title-group.article-title: Risk factors for mortality in children with pertussis and hyperleukocytosis undergoing exchange transfusion: a single-center retrospective cohort study

sec.title: Background
sec.p: Pertussis-related hyperleukocytosis is a major driver of pediatric mortality. While exchange transfusion (ET) improves survival, predictors of death in ET-treated children remain poorly defined. We sought to identify independent predictors of death to refine treatment strategies.

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: A single-center retrospective cohort study analysis of 44 children with pertussis-related hyperleukocytosis treated with ET was conducted. Patients were stratified into survival (n = 27) and mortality (n = 17) groups. Univariate comparisons of clinical, laboratory, and ET-related parameters were performed. Multivariate logistic regression identified independent mortality risk factors.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: The mortality group exhibited a younger median age at onset (55 vs. 103 days, p = 0.006), higher peak white blood cell (WBC) count (82.19 ± 21.95 vs. 68.10 ± 18.78 × 10⁹/L, p = 0.023), and greater incidence of pre-ET cardiovascular failure (94.1% vs. 22.2%, p < 0.001). In multivariable analysis using Firth’s penalized logistic regression, pre-ET cardiovascular failure (OR 53.69, 95% CI 3.63–795.10), higher peak WBC count (OR 1.09 per 1 × 10⁹/L increase, 95% CI 1.02–1.17), and younger age at onset (OR 0.97 per day increase, 95% CI 0.95–0.99) showed significant associations with mortality.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: Younger age at onset, marked leukocytosis, and pre-ET cardiovascular failure were associated with increased mortality in children with pertussis complicated by hyperleukocytosis. These factors may help identify patients at higher risk and highlight the importance of early recognition, close monitoring, and timely supportive management. Further prospective studies with larger sample sizes are warranted to validate these findings and to inform optimized management strategies in this vulnerable population.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Pertussis (whooping cough), caused by Bordetella pertussis, remains a major global health threat despite widespread vaccination efforts. As the fifth leading vaccine-preventable cause of infectious mortality in children worldwide [1], severe pertussis manifests as refractory hypoxemia, cardiogenic shock, and pneumonia, often complicated by hyperleukocytosis—a hallmark of disease severity [2–4]. Elevated WBC (> 30 × 10⁹/L) correlate strongly with pulmonary hypertension (PH) and mortality, with leukocyte-mediated vascular obstruction exacerbating cardiac strain and systemic inflammation [5–6].

ET, traditionally used for neonatal hyperbilirubinemia, has emerged as a life-saving intervention for pertussis-associated hyperleukocytosis since its first reported application in 2004 [6]. By rapidly reducing circulating leukocytes and pertussis toxin concentrations, ET mitigates pulmonary vascular resistance and cardiac dysfunction [6–8]. Clinical studies demonstrate its survival benefits [7, 9]: Rowlands et al. observed a mortality reduction from 45% to 10% with leukoreduction therapies [10], while Berger et al. reported a 64% survival rate in ET-treated cohorts [4]. Despite these advances, mortality persists in 30–40% of cases [4, 11], underscoring unresolved challenges.

Current knowledge gaps hinder optimal clinical practice. First, risk factors for post-ET mortality remain poorly defined, limiting risk stratification and timely intervention. Second, existing studies lack granular details on ET protocols (e.g., volume, rate, blood product ratios), impeding standardized implementation. Furthermore, the interplay between hyperleukocytosis, cardiovascular failure, and inflammatory markers (e.g., neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio, procalcitonin) warrants deeper exploration to refine prognostic models.

This retrospective study addresses these gaps by analyzing 44 pediatric patients with pertussis-related hyperleukocytosis undergoing ET. We aim to: (1) identify independent mortality risk factors through multivariate analysis; (2) delineate ET procedural parameters and complications; and (3) establish evidence-based recommendations to optimize therapeutic protocols. Our findings aim to inform clinical decision-making and improve survival in this high-risk population.

sec.title: Patient selection
sec.p: This single-center retrospective cohort study included patients diagnosed with hyperleukocytosis (WBC count exceeding 30 × 10⁹/L) due to pertussis who underwent ET at the Children’s Hospital of Chongqing Medical University from April 1, 2018, to October 31, 2024. All patients exhibited clinical manifestations of pertussis, which were confirmed through polymerase chain reaction (PCR) or culture methods.
Indications for exchange transfusion.
ET was considered when WBC exceeded the following thresholds and the listed complications were present:

list-item.label: A.
list-item.p: If the WBC count exceeds 30 × 10⁹/ L with respiratory failure, cardiovascular failure or PH;

list-item.label: B.
list-item.p: If the WBC count exceeds 40 × 10⁹/ L with cardiovascular failure or echocardiographic PH;

list-item.label: C.
list-item.p: If the WBC count exceeds 50 × 10⁹/ L with respiratory failure and/or cardiovascular failure;

list-item.label: D.
list-item.p: If the WBC count exceeds 50 × 10⁹/ L with respiratory failure and/or echocardiographic PH.

sec.p: Exclusion criteria comprised patients with severe underlying cardiovascular disease, immunodeficiency, neuromuscular disease, hematological malignancies, and those with incomplete data.

sec.title: Data collection
sec.p: We extracted demographics, clinical data, laboratory and microbiological results, complications, treatment details, ET parameters and outcomes. All data were sourced from the hospital’s clinical data platform and electronic medical record system.

Important preparations before ET include: firstly, establishing peripheral arteriovenous access, with one arterial and two venous lines—one for blood and the other for additional fluids. Secondly, the preparation of blood products, including concentrated red blood cell suspension and fresh frozen plasma, in a ratio of 2:1 or 3:1, adjusted according to pre-exchange hemoglobin (Hb) and hematocrit (HCT) levels.

During the ET procedure, blood was drawn in 50–60 ml increments from the arterial line, with intermittent flushing using 1–5 units of heparin to maintain arterial patency. Blood products were infused through the venous line, starting with half of the red blood cell suspension, followed by fresh frozen plasma, and concluding with the remaining red blood cell suspension. The exchange rate was set at 60–80 mL/kg.h, with a total exchange volume of 80–100 mL/kg. For every 100 ml of blood exchanged, 1 ml of calcium gluconate was continuously infused through a separate venous line to prevent hypocalcemia. Throughout the procedure, key indicators such as blood glucose, calcium levels, coagulation function, and blood pressure were continuously monitored. The protocol described above remained unchanged throughout the study period (April 2018 – October 2024) and was applied uniformly to all enrolled patients; no meaningful variations in blood-product ratio, exchange volume, or infusion rate were introduced over time.

sec.title: Clinical indicators and related definitions
sec.p: Respiratory failure: hypoxemia (PaO₂ < 60 mmHg) and tachypnea (< 1 y: > 60 /min; 1–3 y: > 50 /min) [12]. PH: echocardiographic criteria per 2015 ESC/ERS guidelines [13]. Cardiovascular failure: acute circulatory dysfunction requiring vasoactive support, equivalent to ESC/AHA cardiogenic shock [14], diagnosed by cardiac dysfunction, pulmonary/systemic congestion, sinus tachycardia (< 1 y: > 160/min), or echo evidence of cardiac dysfunction. Hypotension (systolic BP < 5th percentile for age) was recorded when present but was not a prerequisite for the diagnosis of cardiovascular failure in this study.

sec.title: Statistical analysis
sec.p: Statistical analysis was performed using R 4.4.1 statistical analysis software. Normally distributed data are expressed as the mean ± standard deviation (SD) and were compared using the Student’s t test. Non-normally distributed quantitative data are presented as the median (interquartile range, IQR), and group comparisons were made using the Mann-Whitney U test. Categorical data are presented as percentages (%) and analysed using the chi-square test or Fisher’s exact test, as appropriate. To identify factors associated with mortality, multivariable analysis was performed using Firth’s penalized logistic regression to reduce small-sample bias and overfitting risk. Variables were selected based on clinical relevance and supported by evidence of association in univariable analyses, and the number of variables was deliberately restricted due to the limited number of outcome events. Model discrimination was assessed using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC). Internal validation was performed using bootstrap resampling (1,000 resamples), with model refitting in each resample. The 95% confidence interval (CI) for the AUC was derived from the empirical distribution of bootstrap estimates using percentile-based methods. Model calibration was evaluated using a calibration plot comparing predicted probabilities with observed event rates.A two-sided p-value of < 0.05 was considered statistically significant.

sec.title: Ethics
sec.p: This is a retrospective study, with all data derived from routine clinical diagnoses and treatments, involving no additional interventions or experimental procedures, and all personally identifiable information has been removed. Informed consent was therefore waived by the ethics committee due to the study’s retrospective nature. This study adheres to the ethical standards of the Declaration of Helsinki and was approved by the Ethics Committee of the Children’s Hospital of Chongqing Medical University [(2025) ethical review (Research) No. 011 − 001].

sec.title: Demographic characteristics
sec.p: During a 6-year period we enrolled 44 children with pertussis-related hyperleukocytosis who received ET. Their demographic characteristics are shown in Table 1. Females comprised 54.55% of the patients, with 44.44% in the survival group and 70.59% in the mortality group, indicating a significantly higher proportion of females in the mortality group. The median age at onset was 64 days (IQR: 42 to 171.5 days), with 55 days (IQR: 31 to 60 days) in the mortality group and 103 days (IQR: 52.5 to 228 days) in the survival group. The median birth weight was 3.20 kg (IQR: 3.00 to 3.45 kg), with 3.00 kg (IQR: 2.90 to 3.24 kg) in the mortality group and 3.26 kg (IQR: 3.12 to 3.50 kg) in the survival group. Significant differences were observed in age at onset, birth weight and the incidence of onset age < 90 days between the survival and mortality groups. Only 8 patients had received the pertussis vaccine, with 6 in the survival group and 2 in the mortality group. There were no statistically significant differences in vaccination status or doses between the survival and mortality groups.

sec.title: Clinical manifestations and complications
sec.p: The clinical manifestations and complications of the 44 patients are summarized in Table 1. A total of 79.5% of patients (35/44) experienced varying degrees of fever before ET, while 84.1% (37/44) had other pathogens detected in respiratory tests, with 70.5% identified as bacterial pathogens. No statistically significant differences were observed in the incidence of fever, detection rates of other pathogens, or bacterial detection rates between the mortality and survival groups. Regarding complications, 93.2% of patients experienced respiratory failure before ET, with 100% in the mortality group and 88.9% in the survival group. The incidence of PH was 29.5%, with 47.1% in the mortality group and 18.5% in the survival group. Cardiovascular failure occurred in 50% of patients, with 94.1% in the mortality group and 22.2% in the survival group. Significant differences were found in the incidence of PH and cardiovascular failure between the mortality and survival groups. Additionally, three patients in each group experienced seizures.

sec.title: Laboratory test results and clinical treatment
sec.p: The peak WBC count was 73.25 ± 20.96 × 109/L among the 44 patients, with a significantly higher count of 82.19 ± 21.95 × 109/L observed in the mortality group compared to 68.10 ± 18.78 × 109/L in the survival group. The neutrophil/lymphocyte (N/L) ratio was 1.25 (1.08, 1.82) in the mortality group, compared to 0.66 (0.44, 0.96) in the survival group. Notably, 76.5% of patients in the mortality group had an N/L ratio exceeding 1.0, in contrast to only 22.2% in the survival group. Significant differences were observed in both the N/L ratio and the proportion of patients with an N/L ratio exceeding 1 between the two groups. Acute-phase reactants, C-reactive protein (CRP) and procalcitonin (PCT), were elevated in most patients (with normal values defined as CRP < 8 mg/L and PCT < 0.05 ng/ml in this study). The median CRP level was 24.5 (8, 54.5) mg/L, with levels of 50 (29, 63) mg/L in the mortality group and 15 (8, 28) mg/L in the survival group. The median PCT was 0.20 (0.09, 1.44) ng/mL, with values of 1.68 (0.22, 2.79) ng/mL in the mortality group and 0.12 (0.08, 0.46) ng/mL in the survival group. Significant differences in both CRP and PCT levels were observed between the two groups. Regarding treatment, 77.3% (34/44) of patients received invasive mechanical ventilation (IMV), with 94.1% (16/17) of patients in the mortality group undergoing IMV. Additionally, 18 patients (40.9%) received corticosteroid treatment, including 5 (29.4%) in the mortality group and 13 (48.1%) in the survival group. Furthermore, 22 surviving patients received intravenous immunoglobulin(IVIG) treatment, while 4 deceased patients received IVIG. However, the higher utilization of IVIG in survivors is susceptible to confounding by indication and does not imply causality.

sec.title: Comparison of key indicators in the exchange process between the survival and mortality groups
sec.p: In the mortality group, both systolic and diastolic blood pressures measured before and after ET were significantly lower than those in the survival group. Additionally, the WBC count before and after ET was significantly higher in the mortality group compared to the survival group. The proportion of WBC decrease post-ET was 49.29% (38.77, 53.66), with 41.79% (37.42, 58.80) in the mortality group and 50.14% (41.81, 53.31) in the survival group, showing no significant difference between the two groups. Furthermore, no significant differences were observed between the two groups regarding respiratory rate before and after ET, heart rate before and after ET, number of ET cycles, ET volume, the ratio of concentrated red blood cells to fresh plasma, post-ET HCT, duration of ET, blood flow volume during ET, or ET volume to blood volume ratio(see Table 2 for details).

sec.title: Factors associated with mortality
sec.p: Three variables, age at onset, peak WBC count, and cardiovascular failure, were included in the multivariable analysis using Firth’s penalized logistic regression. Pre-ET cardiovascular failure was associated with increased mortality ( odds ratio [OR] 53.69, 95% CI 3.63–795.10). Higher peak WBC count was also associated with mortality (OR 1.09 per 1 × 10⁹/L increase, 95% CI 1.02–1.17). In contrast, younger age at onset was associated with a higher risk of mortality (OR 0.97 per day increase, 95% CI 0.95–0.99) (Table 3 and Supplementary Fig. 1). The model showed good discrimination, with a bootstrap-corrected AUC of 0.968 (95% CI 0.932–0.983) (Fig. 1). Calibration assessment indicated good agreement between predicted probabilities and observed event rates (Supplementary Fig. 2).

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: Although widespread vaccination has reduced pertussis incidence and severity, the disease remains a major global threat to children. A 2018 WHO report documented 151,074 global cases with a 4% mortality [15]. Most deaths occur in children with severe hyperleukocytosis. Rapid and safe reduction of WBC is therefore critical to improve survival. ET significantly reduces peripheral WBC counts and is associated with higher survival rates. In our study, the survival rate was 61.36%, which is comparable to the findings reported by Berger JT et al. [4] and Tingting Shi et al. [11]. We found significant between-group differences in age at onset, sex, birth weight, PH, pre-ET cardiovascular failure, peak WBC, CRP, PCT and peri-ET blood pressure. Further Firth’s logistic regression analysis revealed that pre-ET cardiovascular failure, higher peak WBC count and younger age of onset showed significant associations with mortality in pertussis patients with hyperleukocytosis undergoing ET. These findings provide valuable data and a practical basis for improving the survival rate of hyperleukocytosis pertussis patients receiving ET and optimizing ET strategies.

The proportion of children aged less than 90 days in the mortality group was significantly higher than in the survival group, suggesting an association between younger age and increased disease severity and mortality risk. The pertussis vaccine triggers an immune response against Bordetella pertussis, thereby protecting children from severe disease and death. However, under China’s vaccination schedule, infants typically do not receive the pertussis vaccine until they are 90 days old or older. Additionally, newborns have limited immunity from transplacental antibodies, which is insufficient to protect them during the first three months of life. This may be partly explained by inadequate.pertussis immunity among pregnant women in China. Immunity acquired through natural infection or pertussis vaccination gradually diminishes over time, eventually falling below protective levels, while routine booster pertussis vaccination during pregnancy is currently not implemented in China. As a result, infants under 90 days of age are particularly vulnerable to severe pertussis and death [9, 16–20]. Earlier infant vaccination and maternal booster programmes are urgently needed in China. In response, china has already moved the first dose to 2 months of age [21]. It is hoped that, in the near future, booster pertussis vaccinations for pregnant women will also be implemented.

Our study found that fever and bacterial co-infection are common in hyperleukocytosis pertussis patients, with 79.5% experiencing varying degrees of fever prior to ET and 70.6% showing bacterial pathogens in respiratory tests. However, no significant differences in the incidence of fever or bacterial co-infection were observed between the mortality and survival groups, suggesting that these factors may have limited value in discriminating value for mortality risk in this cohort. In contrast, the N/L ratio, CRP, and PCT levels were significantly higher in the mortality group compared to the survival group. These elevations are consistent with more intense systemic inflammation and more severe tissue injury among non-survivors, predisposing to multiple-organ dysfunction and death. Monitoring these inflammatory markers may may therefore have potential value in risk stratification and clinical assessment.

In our study, we found that the peak WBC count, the incidence of PH, and the incidence of cardiovascular failure were significantly higher in the mortality group compared to the survival group. Additionally, both systolic and diastolic blood pressure before and after ET was significantly lower in the mortality group than in the survival group. These findings suggest potential interactions among hyperleukocytosis, PH, and cardiovascular failure, which may elevate the risk of mortality. Specifically, hyperleukocytosis could increase pulmonary vascular resistance by raising blood viscosity, thereby contributing to the development of PH. The presence of PH significantly exacerbates the burden on the right heart, leading to cardiac dysfunction; as the disease progresses, cardiovascular failure gradually ensues. This progression results in decreased circulatory efficiency, hemodynamic instability, and ultimately hypotension [4, 22]. We observed that combined cardiovascular failure and severe PH almost invariably precede death, reflecting compounded circulatory collapse. This underscores the necessity for vigilant monitoring of these factors in clinical management and the importance of timely intervention to enhance patient prognosis.

Consistent with the univariable findings, the Firth’s logistic regression analysis conducted in this study suggested pre-ET cardiovascular failure, higher peak WBC count, and younger age at onset as factors associated with mortality. The extremely high OR observed for pre-ET cardiovascular failure should be interpreted with caution, as it does not indicate a precise quantitative effect size but largely reflects statistical imprecision inherent to a small-event setting, in which nearly all non-survivors experienced cardiovascular failure prior to ET. Although the prediction model showed reasonable overall discriminative ability and calibration, the effect estimates for individual predictors remain inherently unstable in the context of the present study. Beyond this methodological consideration, cardiovascular failure may also represent a late stage in the pathophysiological cascade of severe pertussis. Larger, multicentre studies are required to derive more stable and generalisable risk estimates.

From a clinical perspective, these findings further suggest that for children with pertussis and marked hyperleukocytosis, early intervention may be warranted rather than postponing treatment until severe complications such as cardiovascular failure, arise. Early intervention may enhance microcirculation, reduce PH, and alleviate cardiac burden, thereby potentially improving patient prognosis [11, 23]. Currently, no standardized criteria exist for therapeutic intervention in pertussis-associated hyperleukocytosis globally. Consequently, further research is essential to develop more scientifically grounded and rational criteria for intervention. On one hand, additional exploration and validation of mortality-associated risk factors are necessary to prevent delays in intervention that could lead to poor prognoses; Conversely, evidence-based thresholds will minimise unnecessary procedures and ET-related adverse events.

In this study, we analyzed several key parameters in volved in the ET process, including exchange volume, frequency, the ratio of concentrated red blood cells to fresh frozen plasma, post-exchange HCT, exchange duration, and blood flow rate during the exchange. The results revealed no statistically significant differences between the mortality and survival groups across these indicators, demonstrating good consistency in the exchange operation process. Furthermore, our findings indicate no direct correlation between the technical factors of ET and patient outcomes. Currently, there are no standardized settings for the key parameters of ET in patients with hyperleukocytosis due to pertussis. Nevertheless, the exchange process outlined in this study offers practical references for future related treatments.

We observed more frequent IVIG administration in survivors, but this association should be viewed with caution. Treatment decisions were made by attending physicians based on clinical impression rather than predefined criteria, creating inherent severity and selection bias. Consequently, the observed difference likely reflects confounding by indication rather than a true protective effect of IVIG, and no causal inference should be drawn from our retrospective data.

This study has several limitations. First, its single-center retrospective design and modest sample size may limit generalizability. Although this represents one of the larger reported ET cohorts of children with pertussis-related hyperleukocytosis undergoing ET, the number of outcome events remained limited. To address this limitation, we deliberately restricted the number of variables included in the multivariable model and applied Firth’s penalised logistic regression to reduce small-sample bias and mitigate potential separation. Model performance was evaluated using internal validation with bootstrap resampling. Nevertheless, the observed associations should be interpreted cautiously, and the model’s discriminative performance should be regarded as exploratory rather than definitive. Despite the limitation, the present findings may still offer clinically relevant insights for early risk stratification and critical care decision-making. In addition, this study was not designed to establish an evidence-based WBC count threshold for intervention. Prospective, multicentre studies with larger cohorts are required to validate these findings, refine risk estimates, and define optimal timing and selection criteria for ET in this vulnerable population.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: This study showed that three factors were associated with mortality among children with pertussis-associated hyperleukocytosis undergoing ET: younger age at onset, higher peak WBC count, and pre-ET cardiovascular failure. These factors may assist early risk stratification in clinical practice. Although ET remains a cornerstone therapy, its effectiveness likely depends on timely initiation before advanced organ dysfunction develops. Our findings suggest two potential implications for clinical practice. Earlier leukoreductive intervention should be considered in young children with marked leukocytosis, although the optimal WBC threshold for initiating ET requires prospective validation. In addition, enhanced cardiovascular monitoring should be prioritised in high-risk patients, including during the post-ET period. Prospective multicentre studies with larger cohorts are needed to validate these findings and to inform evidence-based, risk-adapted management strategies for children with pertussis and hyperleukocytosis.
